raw_case_text:
Case 1: A 35-year-old man, computer technician, with irrelevant past medical history, was admitted to our outpatient clinic at the beginning of October 2012 with a 2-day history of papular and vesicular skin rash. He complained of fever with chills, malaise and sore throat 1 day before the onset of cutaneous symptoms. Moreover, the patient reported close contact with a child suffering from HFMD, during a family party, 1 week before symptoms developed.
Physical examination revealed erythematous papulovesicular lesions on the posterior oropharyngeal structures and multiple erythematous papules followed by vesicular lesions on his palms, soles and perioral zone (fig. 1a, b, fig. 2a). A complete blood count revealed no abnormalities. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was increased to 20 mm/h. Blood chemistry tests were normal, except for the level of C-reactive protein (CRP), which was elevated to 12 mg/l. Syphilis, HIV and hepatitis B and C serologies were negative. The pattern of serum protein electrophoresis was normal, and the initial chest X-ray and ECG demonstrated no pathologic findings.
Viral ribonucleic acid was extracted from vesicular fluid samples (both from the throat and skin) and from plasma. Afterwards, it was amplified with reverse transcription-seminested polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay as described elsewhere, using primers that allow amplification of all known human enteroviruses and identification of the serotypes by amplicon sequencing. The primers used for the seminested step amplified a 376-bp portion of the capsid viral protein 1 (VP1) gene. The amplicon sequencing and comparison to gene database identified Coxsackievirus A6, both from vesicles and plasma.
Histological examination of the skin biopsy from a palmar papule showed orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis with areas of confluent parakeratosis and presence of singular basal and suprabasal keratinocyte necrosis. Moreover, a lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate was present in the superficial dermis up to dermo-epidermal junction. The histological features were consistent with a viral infection.
The patient was diagnosed with HFMD based on characteristic clinical manifestations, positive results of enterovirus PCR analysis, molecular typing for Coxsackievirus A6 and histological findings. Symptomatic treatment with oral paracetamol and lidocaine oral spray was introduced. During a 7-month follow-up, no complications were observed. Skin and mucosal lesions resolved completely. No nail changes have been observed so far, but the child who infected the patient with Coxsackievirus A6 developed onychomadesis 2 months later (fig. 1c).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old male computer technician presented with a 2-day history of a papulovesicular rash on his palms, soles, and perioral area preceded by 1 day of fever, chills, malaise, and sore throat.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In early October 2012, 1 week after close contact at a family party with a child who had hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD), the patient developed 1 day of prodromal fever, chills, malaise, and sore throat followed by a 2-day eruption of papules and vesicles on his palms, soles, perioral skin, and oropharynx.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical history. Epidemiological exposure to a child with HFMD 1 week prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, malaise, sore throat, and palmoplantar/perioral papulovesicular rash.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination revealed erythematous papulovesicular lesions on the posterior oropharynx and multiple erythematous papules and vesicles distributed over the palms, soles, and perioral skin.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC, routine blood chemistry, serum protein electrophoresis, chest X-ray, and ECG were normal; ESR was mildly elevated at 20 mm/h and CRP was elevated at 12 mg/L. Serological tests for syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Palmar papule skin biopsy histopathology showed orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis with focal confluent parakeratosis, individual basal and suprabasal keratinocyte necrosis, and a superficial dermal lymphocytic infiltrate extending to the dermo-epidermal junction. Reverse transcription-seminested PCR and VP1 amplicon sequencing from throat/skin vesicular fluid and plasma identified Coxsackievirus A6.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed adult hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) caused by Coxsackievirus A6 (secondary syphilis excluded via negative syphilis serology and positive enterovirus VP1 RT-PCR/sequencing). Managed symptomatically with oral paracetamol and topical lidocaine oral spray, achieving complete resolution of mucocutaneous lesions without onychomadesis or other complications over 7 months of follow-up.
